title: Commentary: Mostly species but don’t forget floods
content: Reflecting this commentary’s title, we have many articles in this issue focused on species. On a collective personal note, Kilman’s book review of Cruzan’s Looking Down the Tree (https://doi.org/10.1093/biosci/biag050) highlights the author’s entertaining and informative perspective that much of human evolution can be associated with the transition to bipedalism and larger brain size. Certainly, the book will be on my holiday wish list. Grossman’s Viewpoint “Why aren’t we publishing more? The narrative bottleneck in evolutionary biology” (https://doi.org/10.1093/biosci/biag055) provides a thoughtful commentary to the publishing bottlenecks that all of us face and concludes that “the constraint lies not in production, but in interpretation: in the intellectual labor of deciding what our results mean and which claims they justify,” especially in the foundational biodiversity disciplines, which are grounded on conceptual, theoretical, and deeply quantitative approaches. This opinion piece would be a great lab discussion reading. In addition to field stations being a great place to be rejuvenated by your surroundings, colleagues, and supportive of work–life balance (children often fit in well), they play a key role in conservation, as is described by Karubian and colleagues in their Viewpoint, “From policy to practice: field stations as engines of tropical conservation” (https://doi.org/10.1093/biosci/biag078). Our final Viewpoint, “Integration, not replacement: molecular methods and a new equilibrium in taxonomy” (https://doi.org/10.1093/biosci/biag065), by Kollár, provides an assessment of the contribution of molecular approaches to taxonomy and concludes that both organismal and molecular approaches are necessary for our understanding of biodiversity. Kollár’s Viewpoint matches well with the Special Report on DNA bar coding discussed below. Finally, we have two letters furthering the discussion initiated by Barry and colleagues, “Crediting and citing Indigenous Knowledges within research (BioScience, 2026, https://doi.org/10.1093/biosci/biag009), by Ward and colleagues (https://doi.org/10.1093/biosci/biag077) and the response by Barry and colleagues (https://doi.org/10.1093/biosci/biag092).
